We propose a preliminary implementation to measure the "Effective Failure Size" of deep learning ensembles composed of parameter-efficient adapters. The core idea is that if multiple models (adapters) derived from the same base model make errors simultaneously, they are not independent experts, and their combined reliability is lower than assumed. We will use a simplified synthetic vision task with MNIST-like data where we train a fixed pre-trained backbone and attach several distinct LoRA-style adapters to it. Each adapter is trained on slightly different subsets or noise patterns to simulate real-world variance, but crucially shares the same feature extractor weights. After training, we evaluate each adapter's predictions on a held-out test set, specifically focusing on hard examples or distribution-shifted inputs to induce correlated failures. For every sample in the test set, we record a binary failure indicator for each adapter (1 if wrong, 0 if right). We then compute the average failure rate across all N adapters per sample and calculate the variance of this average failure indicator over the entire test set. Using the formula provided, $E_{eff} = N / (N \cdot Var(\bar{I}_{fail}) + \epsilon)$, we derive the effective independent ensemble size. A low value compared to N indicates high correlation among failures. This metric serves as our primary diagnostic for whether nominal diversity translates to functional independence.

To validate the hypothesis that ensemble members derived from similar bases exhibit correlated failures, we will construct a controlled synthetic experiment. We generate a binary classification dataset with inherent spurious correlations between features and labels, ensuring that models trained on this data will likely fail together on specific slices. We train three distinct simple neural network classifiers: one using standard random initialization (baseline), and two others initialized with weights derived from a shared "pre-trained" checkpoint to simulate adapter-like dependencies. For each model, we compute predictions on a held-out test set containing both in-distribution samples and shifted samples where the spurious correlation is reversed or absent. We then calculate pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients of the binary failure indicators (incorrect vs correct predictions) across all model pairs. Finally, we estimate the effective independent ensemble size ($N_{eff}$) using the formula $N_{eff} = \frac{(\sum f_i)^2}{\sum f_i^2}$, where $f_i$ is the vector of failure counts per sample for member $i$, adjusted by variance-based scaling if necessary, though direct count-based estimation suffices for initial insight. This setup allows us to compare the nominal ensemble size (3) against the measured effective size, expecting lower independence for the shared-base adapters. The code includes robust logging of metrics, saves intermediate prediction matrices, and visualizes the correlation heatmaps.
